title: The Multiple You Get Is Set Years Before You Ever List the Business
excerpt: The multiple a buyer offers is rarely set in the six months before a sale. It reflects years of earnings consistency, customer spread and owner independence built well before that.
content:
Most owners treat the decision to sell as the starting gun for preparing the business to be sold. The reporting gets tidied, a valuer or broker gets a call, and there is a quiet assumption that six months of clean presentation can fix whatever the numbers show. For a good part of what actually sets the multiple, that timing is already too late.

A buyer, or the valuer working on their behalf, is not pricing one year of profit. They are pricing the pattern sitting behind it. How consistent the earnings have been across several years, how much of the revenue still depends on the owner personally, how concentrated the customer base has become, and how well the systems would survive a change of hands. None of that shows up convincingly in a single year of tidy financial statements, no matter how well they are presented.

October is a good month to notice this, even for owners who have no intention of selling soon. It carries the kind of forward looking energy that EOFY doesn't, a chance to look three to five years out rather than just close the books on the year behind.

What a Buyer Is Actually Pricing

A valuation is, underneath the formulas, a judgement about risk. Earnings that have moved in a predictable pattern across several years attract a more confident multiple than the same headline profit produced by one strong, slightly unusual year, because the pattern is what tells a buyer whether this year was the new normal or simply a good one. Add backs get more credibility when they follow a consistent logic year after year rather than appearing selectively in the year the business is being sold. Owner dependence is judged by how the business performed during a period the owner genuinely stepped back, not by a confident claim that the team could manage without them. None of these are things a business can demonstrate for the first time in the six months before a sale, because a buyer is really asking what the business has already proven, not what it might be capable of.

Why the Rush Job Rarely Moves the Number

A pre sale clean up is genuinely useful. It tidies presentation, resolves loose ends in the accounts, and removes obvious distractions for a buyer doing due diligence. What it cannot do is manufacture three years of consistent trading history, suddenly diversify a customer base that has drifted toward one or two large accounts, or prove the business runs well without the owner in a matter of months. Those patterns take years to build, and buyers, or the valuers pricing the business on their behalf, are specifically looking for the years, not the months. A business that starts documenting its systems, spreading its customer base and steadying its reporting only once a sale is being contemplated is usually asking three years of work to happen in the time available before due diligence begins, and it tends to show.

What Starting Early Actually Looks Like

Starting early rarely means anything dramatic. It usually means a consistent monthly reporting rhythm instead of an annual scramble, add backs that are documented the same way every year rather than reconstructed at sale time, and a deliberate, patient effort to bring the next largest customer or two into the business so no single relationship carries too much of the revenue. It also means an honest look at which parts of the business still run through the owner's personal relationships and judgement, and a plan to document or delegate them well before a buyer ever asks the question. An Exit Readiness Diagnostic is a useful way to see this clearly, since it scores the business across the specific dimensions a buyer will eventually judge it on, whether a sale is imminent or still years away.

None of this requires treating the business differently to how a well run business should already be managed. That is the point. The habits that lift a future multiple are largely indistinguishable from good general management in the years before a sale is ever on the table, which is exactly why they are so easy to put off and so valuable to start now, while there is no buyer in the room and no deadline forcing the pace. For an owner curious about where the business sits today, an indicative read on value is a reasonable place to begin that conversation.

By the time a business is genuinely for sale, the multiple on offer is largely a reflection of decisions made years earlier, not the six months of polish applied at the end. October's planning mood is as good a prompt as any to ask which of those years is starting now.

faqs.q: How many years of financial history does a business valuation typically need?
faqs.a: Valuers and buyers generally want to see several years of trading history, not just the most recent one, because a single strong year does not confirm whether the result is the new normal or a one off. The pattern across those years, rather than any single figure, is what a buyer is really pricing.

faqs.q: Can I improve my business valuation in the months before I sell?
faqs.a: You can improve presentation quickly, tidying accounts and resolving loose ends before due diligence begins. What takes longer is the underlying pattern a buyer prices, such as customer concentration, owner dependence and earnings consistency, which is why an Exit Readiness Diagnostic is more useful well before a sale than in the months right before one.

faqs.q: What makes a business too dependent on its owner for a buyer's liking?
faqs.a: It usually shows up as key relationships, pricing decisions or operational knowledge that sit with the owner rather than being documented or shared across the team. Buyers test this by asking how the business performed during any period the owner stepped back, which is a harder thing to demonstrate convincingly than to simply claim.

faqs.q: How much does customer concentration affect what a business is worth in Australia?
faqs.a: A business where one or two customers make up a large share of revenue is generally seen as carrying more risk, since losing that relationship would materially change the numbers. Spreading revenue across a broader customer base over time is one of the more reliable ways to support a stronger multiple.

faqs.q: When should an Australian SME owner start preparing their business for a future sale?
faqs.a: Years before it is actually needed, even if a sale is not firmly planned. The habits that support a stronger multiple, consistent reporting, documented systems and a spread customer base, take years to bed in and are worth building regardless of whether a sale happens, since they also make the business easier to run day to day.

faqs.q: What is an indicative business valuation and why would I get one early?
faqs.a: It is a defensible read on what the business is likely worth today, built across several methodologies, along with the biggest value drivers and detractors behind that number. Getting an indicative business valuation years before a planned sale gives an owner a clear baseline and enough runway to work on what is actually moving the number.
